title: The Alien Intelligence Next Door
focus: Hedging and impersonal structures in academic English
paragraphs: If one were to design an intelligent creature from scratch, it seems unlikely that the result would resemble an octopus. It has no skeleton, lives for barely a year or two in most species, and receives no instruction whatsoever from its parents, who typically die before their young hatch. Yet there is a growing body of evidence to suggest that octopuses are capable of problem-solving, play and perhaps even something approaching individual personality. They would appear, in short, to be the closest thing to an alien mind that we are ever likely to meet.

The anecdotes are well known among those who work with them. Octopuses have been observed unscrewing jars from the inside, squirting jets of water at laboratory lights they apparently dislike, and escaping from their tanks at night to raid neighbouring ones before returning, as if nothing had happened, by morning. Such stories are entertaining, but they are, it must be acknowledged, difficult to interpret. Anecdote is not evidence, and there is a well-documented tendency for researchers to read human motives into animal behaviour.

More controlled studies, however, tend to support the impression of a flexible intelligence. Octopuses can learn to navigate mazes, distinguish between shapes and, according to some experiments, recognise individual humans, reacting differently to keepers who have treated them kindly and those who have not. It has also been reported that some individuals use coconut shells as portable shelters, carrying them across the sea floor for later use, a behaviour which, if confirmed, would arguably qualify as tool use.

What makes these findings particularly intriguing is the octopus's evolutionary history. The last common ancestor of octopuses and humans is generally thought to have been a small, worm-like creature that lived more than five hundred million years ago and possessed, at most, a very simple nervous system. It follows that whatever intelligence the octopus has evolved independently of our own. If that is the case, it would suggest that complex minds are not a single, unlikely accident but a solution that evolution may arrive at more than once.

The architecture of that mind is strikingly unfamiliar. Of an octopus's five hundred million or so neurons, roughly two-thirds are located not in its brain but in its arms. Each arm appears to be capable of a degree of independent action: an arm that has been severed will, for a time, continue to reach for food and pass it towards where the mouth would have been. Quite what it is like to be such a creature, if it is like anything at all, is a question that is perhaps impossible to answer, but it has led some philosophers to speculate that octopus experience may be distributed in ways that have no human equivalent.

Caution is clearly warranted. Much of the research has been carried out on a small number of species, often in artificial conditions, and the extent to which laboratory behaviour reflects life in the wild remains uncertain. There is also a risk that the octopus's undeniable charm encourages more generous interpretations than the data strictly justify. Nonetheless, the weight of evidence has been considered sufficient for several countries to extend animal welfare protections to octopuses used in research, a development that would have seemed improbable only a generation ago.

That shift raises uncomfortable questions about the growing interest in octopus farming. Critics argue that confining a solitary, curious and apparently easily bored animal in crowded tanks would be difficult to reconcile with what is now known about its needs. Supporters of the industry counter that welfare standards can be developed. Which view will prevail is, for now, an open question. What seems reasonably clear is that the octopus has forced scientists to reconsider some long-held assumptions about where, and in what form, intelligence might be found.

title: The Last Keeper
focus: Aspect and nuance: perfect and continuous forms
paragraphs: By the time the letter arrived, Agnes had been keeping the light on Carrow Head for thirty-one years, and she had been expecting it for at least ten of them. The envelope was thick and official, the kind that is never good news. She left it unopened on the kitchen table while she climbed the hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room, as she had done every evening since her husband died, and lit the lamp, which no longer needed her to light it.

That was the joke, of course, and she had been telling it to herself for years. The light had been automatic since 1998. A computer in a city she had never visited switched it on at dusk and off at dawn, and a technician came out twice a year to replace whatever had worn out. Agnes's official title had long since changed from 'keeper' to 'attendant', and her duties had shrunk to keeping the paint fresh, the windows clean and the visitors' book up to date. But she had gone on climbing the stairs at dusk, and she had gone on pressing the switch that no longer did anything, because it seemed wrong to let the light come on by itself with nobody there to see it.

She opened the letter the next morning. It was polite and regretful and full of phrases such as 'operational review' and 'transition arrangements'. The cottage was to be sold. Her position would end in March. In recognition of her long service, she was invited to a small ceremony at which she would be presented with a framed photograph of the lighthouse.
'A photograph,' she said aloud, to the cat. 'As if I'd forget what it looks like.'

She had been thinking, lately, about the keepers who had come before her. There had been a logbook going back to 1861, now kept in a museum on the mainland, and she had read it so often that she knew whole entries by heart. Storm all night. Lamp maintained. Brig sighted SW, in difficulty, could do nothing. One keeper, in the winter of 1883, had written the same words every day for six weeks: Nothing to report. Agnes had always found those entries the most moving of all. She imagined him sitting where she sat, watching the same grey water, having nothing to report and reporting it anyway, because that was what keepers did.

In the weeks that followed, people kept telling her how lucky she was. She would be closer to the shops. She would have neighbours. She would not have to climb those stairs in her seventies. She knew they meant well, and she smiled and agreed, and did not try to explain that she had never once, in thirty-one years, thought of the stairs as something she had to do.

On her last evening, she climbed them slowly, counting as she always did. The sea was calm, the sky a deepening violet. She stood by the switch and waited, and at the moment the computer in the distant city decided that dusk had arrived, she pressed it, and the light came on. It would have come on anyway. She knew that. But for one more night, it had not come on alone.

She wrote a final entry in the visitors' book before she left, in the careful hand she had always used for the logbook. She had considered a number of things to say: something about the sea, perhaps, or the years. In the end, she wrote only four words, and they were not her own.
Nothing to report. Lamp maintained.

title: What the Open-Plan Office Took Away
paragraphs: It was the noise-cancelling headphones that first gave it away. Walk through almost any modern office and you will see them: large, padded, often expensive, worn by people who are not listening to anything at all. What they are doing is building a wall. In workplaces designed to remove walls, employees have quietly reconstructed them, one pair of ears at a time.

The open-plan office was sold to us as a revolution in collaboration. Knock down the partitions, the argument went, and ideas would flow freely between desks; junior staff would learn by overhearing their seniors; the hierarchy symbolised by the corner office would dissolve into a democratic sea of shared tables. What actually happened was rather different. Several studies that tracked employees before and after a move to open-plan layouts found that face-to-face interaction fell, sometimes dramatically, while email and instant messaging rose. When everyone can hear everything, it turns out, people stop saying very much out loud.

It is not collaboration, however, that I most mourn. It is concentration. The kind of work that most of us are paid to do, writing, analysing, designing, solving problems, depends on sustained stretches of attention that open offices make almost impossible. Research on interruptions suggests that it can take many minutes to return fully to a complex task after being distracted, and that a working day broken into fragments produces work that is not only slower but measurably worse. What an open office offers in abundance is precisely the kind of interruption that most damages this work: the overheard phone call, the colleague who 'just has a quick question', the conversation two desks away about last night's football.

Why, then, have they proved so durable? The honest answer, I suspect, is cost. It is the price of floor space, rather than any evidence about productivity, that has driven most of the redesigns of the past thirty years. An open office can accommodate considerably more people per square metre than one divided into rooms, and the language of collaboration has provided a flattering justification for what is, at heart, an accounting decision.

None of this means that the alternative is a return to rows of closed doors. What many workers seem to want is not isolation but choice: a quiet room when they need to think, a shared space when they need to talk, and the freedom to move between them without explaining themselves. The most thoughtful recent designs reflect this, offering a variety of spaces rather than a single model imposed on everyone.

Where these designs succeed, it is usually because they treat silence as a resource rather than a luxury. One firm I visited had introduced a simple rule: certain areas of the floor were designated for focused work, and conversation there was simply not permitted. The initial reaction was scepticism. Within months, those areas were the most sought-after in the building, and managers reported that the quality of written reports had noticeably improved.

What strikes me most about the open-plan experiment is how long it took us to admit that it was not working. Employees had been signalling their discomfort for years, through headphones, through working from home whenever possible, through booking meeting rooms simply to be alone. It was only when productivity data became impossible to ignore that organisations began to listen. Perhaps the lesson is broader than office design. When people go to great lengths to recreate something you have taken away, it is usually a sign that they needed it.

title: Carrying a Book Across the Water
focus: Ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, one)
paragraphs: Lucía Ferrer has translated more than forty novels from English into Spanish, and a handful in the other direction. We met in a café near her flat, where she had been working since six that morning on a particularly stubborn paragraph. 'Three sentences,' she said. 'Three days. That's not unusual, I'm afraid.'

Q: Do readers realise how much of a translated novel is, in a sense, yours? A: I hope not, frankly. If they did, I'd have failed. The ideal is that they forget there was a translator at all, and most of the time they do. But every sentence involves dozens of choices the author never had to make, because the author was working in one language and I'm working in two. Sometimes the choices are tiny, sometimes they're enormous. Usually they're both at once.

Q: Can you give an example of an enormous one? A: Humour is the obvious one. A pun almost never survives the journey. You can try to find an equivalent, or you can let it go and make the reader laugh somewhere else, a few lines later, where the original didn't. I tend to do the latter, though some translators would say I shouldn't. Then there are dialects. If a character in a Scottish novel speaks broad Glaswegian, do you give her an Andalusian accent? Some translators do so. I'd rather not, because suddenly she's from Seville, and the whole novel has shifted three thousand kilometres.

Q: So what do you do instead? A: I try to find a register rather than a place. Something that sounds informal, working-class, slightly rough, without pointing to any particular map. It's never entirely satisfactory. But then, no solution is. The question isn't whether you lose something. You always do. The question is whether you lose the right thing.

Q: Do authors ever object? A: Occasionally. Most don't read Spanish, so they can't. The ones who do are usually generous. I had one, a very fine novelist, who sent me forty pages of notes on my first draft, all of them perfectly polite and most of them wrong. I accepted a few, not many. He was disappointed, I think, but he wrote to me afterwards to say the reviews had been better in Spain than at home, and he supposed that meant something.

Q: Is translation an art or a craft? A: Both, obviously, but I prefer to call it a craft, because the word 'art' makes people expect inspiration, and translation is mostly patience. You read the original so many times that you begin to hear it, and then you try to write the book the author would have written had they been born in Madrid instead of Manchester. You never quite succeed. Nobody does.

Q: Are you worried about machine translation? A: For instruction manuals, yes, and I don't think I should be, because nobody went into this to translate manuals. For novels, less so. A machine can produce a sentence that is correct. What it can't yet do is decide which of five correct sentences is the right one for this character, on this page, after what happened in chapter three. Perhaps it will one day. I hope not, but I suspect so.

Q: What's the paragraph that's been taking you three days? A: A man describing his father's hands. It's very simple in English. It's simple in Spanish, too, but it's a different simple, and I haven't found it yet. I will, eventually. Or I'll find one that's close enough and spend the next ten years wishing I'd found a better one. That's the job.

title: The Mineral That Built Empires
paragraphs: Sprinkled on chips, dissolved in soup, scattered on icy pavements, salt has become so cheap and so abundant that it is difficult to imagine it ever being worth fighting over. Yet for most of recorded history, salt was among the most valuable commodities on earth. Needed by every human body and essential for preserving food in the centuries before refrigeration, it shaped trade routes, filled royal treasuries and, on more than one occasion, provoked rebellion.

The reason is straightforward. Before the advent of modern preservation, meat and fish left untreated would spoil within days. Packed in salt, or soaked in brine, they could last for months, making it possible to feed armies on the march, sailors on long voyages and whole cities through the winter. A society lacking reliable access to salt was, in a very real sense, a society living from harvest to harvest. Those controlling its supply therefore possessed enormous power.

Some of the earliest large-scale industries grew up around salt production. In ancient China, workers drilling hundreds of metres into the ground extracted brine using bamboo pipes, boiling it over fires fuelled by natural gas rising from the same wells. Taxes levied on the trade became one of the state's principal sources of revenue, financing, among other things, the construction of defensive walls. Recognising its importance, successive dynasties tightened their control, at times establishing a full state monopoly.

Elsewhere, salt travelled vast distances. Caravans crossing the Sahara carried slabs of rock salt cut from desert mines southwards to the markets of West Africa, returning with gold, ivory and other goods. Accounts written by medieval travellers describe towns built entirely from blocks of salt, their inhabitants dependent on supplies of food brought in from hundreds of kilometres away. In such places, it was said, salt was exchanged for gold almost weight for weight, a claim probably exaggerated but revealing nonetheless.

Europe, too, organised much of its economic life around the mineral. Cities situated near salt deposits, or controlling the routes along which salt was transported, grew wealthy on the proceeds. Fishing fleets operating in the North Sea depended on vast quantities of salt to preserve their catch, and the competition to secure it shaped alliances and conflicts between trading powers. Words still in everyday use bear witness to this history: the term 'salary' is often said to derive from the Latin for salt, although the precise connection remains disputed by scholars.

Because it was so essential, salt was also an obvious target for taxation, and taxes imposed on a necessity tend to fall hardest on the poor. In France, a much-resented salt tax, requiring households in some regions to buy a fixed quantity at prices set by the state, became a lasting symbol of royal injustice and contributed to the grievances that preceded the Revolution. In the twentieth century, a march to the sea organised in protest against a colonial salt monopoly in India drew worldwide attention, turning the simple act of collecting salt from the shore into a gesture of defiance.

What finally ended salt's long reign was not politics but technology. The development of new extraction methods in the nineteenth century, combined with railways capable of moving heavy goods cheaply, caused prices to collapse. Refrigeration then removed much of the demand for salt as a preservative. Within a few generations, a substance once guarded by soldiers had become something people threw on roads in winter.

Looking at a salt cellar on a café table today, it is easy to forget all this. But the story of salt offers a useful reminder that value is rarely intrinsic. It depends on scarcity, on need and on who controls the supply, and what seems trivially cheap to one generation may have been worth an empire to another.

title: Cooling the Overheated City
paragraphs: ## Summary This report examines the causes and consequences of the urban heat island effect, the tendency of cities to be significantly warmer than the surrounding countryside, and evaluates a range of measures available to municipal authorities. Its principal conclusion is that a combination of low-cost interventions, implemented consistently across neighbourhoods, can achieve a substantial reduction in summer temperatures, with corresponding benefits for public health.

## Causes The intensification of heat in urban areas is attributable to several interrelated factors. The replacement of vegetation and soil with asphalt, concrete and brick results in the absorption of large quantities of solar energy during the day and its gradual release at night. The narrowness of many streets, combined with the height of surrounding buildings, limits the circulation of air and the escape of heat. In addition, the concentration of vehicles, air-conditioning units and industrial activity contributes a considerable volume of waste heat. In the city centre examined for this report, night-time temperatures during the hottest week of last summer exceeded those recorded in nearby rural areas by up to seven degrees.

## Consequences The health implications are serious. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures, particularly the absence of relief at night, is associated with a marked increase in hospital admissions and mortality among elderly people, young children and those with chronic illnesses. The distribution of this risk is uneven. Residents of densely built, low-income districts, characterised by a scarcity of trees and green space and by poorly insulated housing, experience the greatest exposure while possessing the fewest resources for adaptation. There is also a significant economic dimension: the rise in demand for cooling places considerable strain on electricity networks and raises household energy costs.
## Possible measures A number of interventions have been evaluated in comparable cities.

Tree planting and green space: The expansion of the urban tree canopy is among the most effective measures available. Shade from mature trees can reduce surface temperatures dramatically, while evaporation from leaves cools the surrounding air. The principal limitation is time, since newly planted trees require many years to reach maturity.

Reflective surfaces: The application of light-coloured coatings to roofs and pavements reduces the absorption of solar energy. The low cost of this measure and the speed of its implementation make it particularly attractive, although concerns have been raised regarding glare.

Water features and permeable paving: The introduction of fountains, restored streams and paving that allows rainwater to soak into the ground contributes to cooling through evaporation, with the additional benefit of a reduction in flood risk.

Building regulations: The inclusion of shading, insulation and ventilation requirements in planning rules for new construction offers long-term benefits, although its impact on the existing building stock is limited.
## Recommendations On the basis of the evidence reviewed, it is recommended that the authority:
(a) give priority in its tree-planting programme to the districts identified as most vulnerable, rather than distributing new trees evenly across the city;
(b) undertake the immediate application of reflective coatings to the roofs of schools, clinics and other public buildings;
(c) establish a network of 'cool spaces', such as libraries and community centres, offering free access to shaded and air-conditioned areas during heatwaves;
(d) carry out an annual assessment of the effectiveness of these measures, with the publication of the results.

## Conclusion The urban heat island effect is not an unavoidable consequence of city life but, to a considerable extent, the product of design choices. Its mitigation therefore lies largely within the authority's control. Given the projected increase in the frequency and severity of heatwaves, the adoption of the measures outlined above should be regarded not as an optional improvement but as a matter of urgency.

title: The Girl Who Was to Be Champion
focus: Future forms in the past (was to, was about to, would)
paragraphs: When Mireille Ndiaye won her country's adult chess championship at the age of eleven, the newspapers knew exactly what story to tell. She was to be the first world champion from her region, the coach of the national team declared. She would play in the great tournaments of Europe and Asia. Within a decade, one commentator predicted, she would be a household name. Mireille, who at the time was mostly interested in horses, read the articles with polite bewilderment and went back to her homework.

For the next five years, the predictions seemed to be coming true. She became a grandmaster at fifteen, one of the youngest ever to do so. Sponsors arrived, followed by an agent, a nutritionist and a team of analysts who prepared her openings with the meticulousness of military planners. She travelled more in a single year than most adults do in a lifetime. She was, as she later put it, 'living inside a prophecy'.

The difficulty with prophecies is that they leave very little room for the person they describe. By sixteen, Mireille was spending up to ten hours a day studying chess. She had stopped riding; she had lost touch with most of her school friends; she had begun, she recalls, to experience every game as a test she was about to fail, rather than a contest she might win. Her results remained excellent. Her enjoyment, quietly, had disappeared.

The crisis came at a tournament in which she was expected to qualify for the world championship cycle. She was about to make her twentieth move in a winning position when she found that she could not remember why she was playing at all. She resigned the game, to the astonishment of her opponent, and withdrew from the event the same evening. Her team assumed it was a temporary lapse. It was not. Within a month, she had announced that she was taking an indefinite break from competitive chess.

The reaction was harsh. Some called her ungrateful; others suggested, less kindly, that she had never had the temperament for the top level. The coach who had first proclaimed her destiny said that he was 'deeply disappointed'. Few people asked what she wanted. 'Everyone had a future for me,' she says now. 'Nobody had asked if it was mine.'

What followed was, by the standards of the prophecy, a failure. She went to university, studied veterinary medicine and now runs a small practice treating, among others, horses. She played no serious chess for almost eight years. Then, gradually, she started again, first online, anonymously, and later at a local club where nobody seemed to care who she had once been. She found, to her surprise, that she loved the game again.

She was never to become world champion. Her rating today is lower than it was at sixteen, and she has no ambition to raise it. But she now coaches a group of talented children at her club, and she is careful, she says, about what she tells them. She does not talk about destinies. She talks about the pleasure of a well-played endgame, the value of a wasted afternoon, and the importance of having something in one's life that has nothing to do with winning.

Was the prophecy wrong? In a narrow sense, yes. In another sense, Mireille suggests, it was simply asking the wrong question. 'They wanted to know how far I would go,' she says. 'I'd rather they'd asked where I wanted to go. I would have told them. It just took me a long time to find out.'

title: Review: Brasa, a Restaurant That Tries Very Hard
focus: Intensifiers, downtoners and gradable vs ungradable adjectives
paragraphs: There is a particular kind of restaurant that makes you feel faintly guilty for being hungry. Brasa, which opened last spring in a converted warehouse near the river, is one of them. The lighting is very dim, the staff are extremely earnest, and the menu, which is not so much a list of dishes as a short philosophical essay, informs you that the kitchen 'works in dialogue with fire'. I have nothing against fire. I simply wanted dinner.

Dinner, at Brasa, means a tasting menu of fourteen courses, priced at a figure I will not repeat here in case you are eating. There is no alternative. You may inform the staff of allergies, and they will be absolutely charming about it, but you may not, as far as I could establish, simply order a plate of something and go home.

To be fair, some of what follows is genuinely superb. An early course of grilled leeks, blackened outside and almost impossibly sweet within, served with a sauce of smoked hazelnuts, was utterly delicious, the kind of dish you remember for weeks. A single scallop, cooked for seconds over embers and dressed with nothing but brown butter and lemon, was quite perfect, in the ungradable sense of the word: there was nothing whatsoever to add or take away.

The problems begin when the kitchen's ambition outruns its judgement, which it does fairly often. A 'deconstructed' potato, presented as a powder, a foam and a single crisp, was moderately interesting and entirely unsatisfying; it is a rare achievement to make a potato less pleasurable than a potato. A course of fermented plums with pine-needle ice was slightly too clever by half, and a lamb dish, though beautifully cooked, arrived buried under so many garnishes that I spent the first minute excavating it. None of these was a disaster. All were somewhat less than the sum of their very expensive parts.

Then there is the pacing. Fourteen courses served over three and a half hours leaves a great deal of time for explanation, and the staff use all of it. Each dish is introduced with a short speech about its origins, its farmer and, in one case, its 'emotional temperature'. The first few of these are rather charming. By the eleventh, I was fairly desperate for a plate that arrived in silence.

It would be unfair to dismiss Brasa entirely, and I do not wish to. The kitchen is clearly talented, the ingredients are exceptional, and when the cooks trust them, the results are absolutely remarkable. The wine list is thoughtful and, by the standards of the room, reasonably priced. The service, for all its earnestness, is warm and attentive.

But a restaurant is not only a stage for a chef's ideas; it is a place where people come to eat and to talk to each other. Brasa sometimes forgets this. It is so very keen to impress that it occasionally neglects to please, and there is a difference. The best dishes I ate here were the simplest, and the simplest were the ones that seemed least interested in being admired.

Would I go back? Possibly, if they introduced a shorter menu, or simply let me order the leeks and the scallop and leave before the plums. At present, Brasa is a fairly good restaurant trying extremely hard to be a great one. With a little less effort, it might succeed.

title: The Forger's Fingerprint
focus: Modals of speculation and deduction (present, past, future)
paragraphs: For almost forty years, a small landscape painting hung in the dining room of a provincial museum, labelled as the work of a celebrated nineteenth-century master. Visitors admired it; scholars cited it; it appeared on postcards sold in the gift shop. Then, during routine conservation work, a technician noticed something odd. A pigment in the sky, a particular shade of blue, contained a compound that was not manufactured until the 1930s, several decades after the artist's death. Either the master had somehow acquired paint from the future, or the painting could not be his.

It must have been an uncomfortable morning for the curators. Forgeries are, in one sense, a museum's worst nightmare: they cast doubt not only on a single object but on the judgement of everyone who has vouched for it. Yet they are also more common than most institutions care to admit. Estimates vary widely, and are necessarily speculative, but some specialists believe that a significant proportion of the works circulating on the art market may be wrongly attributed, whether through deliberate fraud or honest error.

How could so many experts have been deceived for so long? Part of the answer lies in what forgers choose to copy. The most successful rarely reproduce famous works, which would be recognised immediately. Instead, they create 'new' paintings in the style of an established artist, often filling a gap in the known record: a missing period, a subject the artist is documented as having painted but which has never been found. Such works can't be compared directly with an original, because no original exists. They need only be plausible, and they will often be accompanied by a convincing history of ownership, itself forged.

Expectation plays a role too. A scholar who has spent years studying an artist may well see what she hopes to see, particularly when a discovery would crown a career. The forger, in effect, collaborates with his victims' desires. The landscape in the provincial museum, it later emerged, had been bought at a time when the institution was eager to expand its collection of nineteenth-century art, and its arrival was greeted with considerable fanfare. Nobody, it seems, had wanted to look too closely.

Technology has changed the balance considerably. Analysis of pigments, canvas fibres and the chemical composition of paint layers can now reveal anachronisms invisible to the naked eye. Infrared imaging can expose underdrawings, the preliminary sketches beneath the paint, which in genuine works tend to show hesitation and correction, and in copies often look suspiciously confident. Some researchers are experimenting with algorithms trained to recognise the characteristic brushwork of individual painters, although such systems are still some way from being accepted as reliable evidence.

Forgers, of course, adapt. A sophisticated forger today will use period canvases, scraped of their original images, and will grind his own pigments from historically appropriate materials. He might even study the scientific literature on authentication in order to avoid its traps. It would be naive to imagine that the contest between detection and deception will ever be decisively won. Each new method of analysis is likely to be followed, sooner or later, by a new method of evasion.

As for the landscape, it has not been destroyed. The museum, after some debate, decided to keep it on display, relabelled as a forgery and accompanied by an explanation of how it was discovered. It has, by all accounts, become one of the most popular objects in the collection. Visitors who once glanced at it in passing now stand in front of it for minutes at a time, examining the sky. Its creator will probably never be identified. Whoever he was, he can hardly have imagined that his work would one day be admired precisely for being fake.

title: In Praise of Boredom
focus: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials
paragraphs: Never before have human beings had so many ways of avoiding boredom, and rarely have we been so anxious about it. The smartphone, the streaming service and the endless scroll have made it possible to fill every spare moment, from the queue at the supermarket to the thirty seconds it takes for the kettle to boil. Not once in a typical day, for many of us, are we left with nothing to look at. This essay is an attempt to suggest that we may have lost something in the process.

Boredom has an unenviable reputation. It is associated with idleness, restlessness and, in children, with the kind of behaviour that ends in broken windows. Psychologists have linked chronic boredom to poor concentration, risk-taking and low mood. Little wonder, then, that we treat it as a problem to be solved, and that entire industries have grown up promising to solve it.

Yet occasional boredom, as distinct from the chronic kind, may serve a purpose. Some researchers have suggested that it acts as a signal, a kind of mental discomfort that tells us our current activity is not meeting our needs and pushes us to look for something more meaningful. Seen in this light, boredom is not a malfunction but a motivator. Only when we are allowed to feel it, the argument goes, do we have a reason to change what we are doing.

There is also some evidence, though it is far from conclusive, that boredom can encourage creative thought. In a frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently came up with more inventive answers to a problem-solving exercise than those who had not. The explanation offered was that boredom sends the mind wandering, and that a wandering mind makes connections a focused one does not. Not until the external world falls quiet, perhaps, does the internal one begin to speak.

Writers and artists have long understood this intuitively. Many have described their best ideas arriving not at the desk but in moments of apparent emptiness: on long walks, during train journeys, in the bath. Such moments were once an unavoidable part of life. Now they must be actively defended, and few of us defend them. No sooner does a pause appear than we reach for a screen to fill it.

I should not want to romanticise this. Boredom can be miserable, and there is nothing noble about enduring a dull meeting or a delayed flight. Nor am I suggesting that we abandon our devices, which bring genuine pleasure and connection. Under no circumstances would I wish to return to an era in which the only alternative to boredom was more boredom. The point is not that boredom is good in itself, but that the instant elimination of every empty moment may deprive us of whatever benefits it brings.

What might a modest defence of boredom look like in practice? It could be as simple as leaving the phone in a pocket while waiting for a bus, or taking a walk without headphones, or allowing children an afternoon with nothing planned. Such experiments are, admittedly, small. But only by conducting them can we discover what our minds do when they are not being constantly fed.

Seldom do we ask what our attention is for. We treat it as something to be spent, and we allow others to compete for it. Perhaps it would be worth, now and then, leaving a little of it unspent, simply to see what grows in the space. The answer may be nothing at all. Or it may, on a good day, be the best idea we have had in months.

title: An Open Letter on the Future of Saltmere
focus: Mixed and inverted conditionals (Should…, Were…, Had…)
paragraphs: To the residents of Saltmere, and to the County Council,

We are writing as members of the Saltmere Coastal Forum, a group of residents, fishermen, scientists and business owners who have spent the past two years studying the future of our village. Our conclusions are not easy to write, and they will not be easy to read. We believe, however, that you deserve to hear them plainly.

The cliffs on which the northern half of Saltmere stands are retreating. They have always done so; the village church, as many of you know, once stood three fields further inland than its ruins do now. What has changed is the pace. Over the past twenty years, the cliff edge has moved back by an average of more than a metre a year, and in the storms of last winter we lost almost six metres in a single night. Had the sea wall at Cliff Road not been reinforced in 2015, the Henderson family's house would now be on the beach.

We understand the instinct to fight. Many of us share it. But we must be honest about the cost. The engineers who advised us estimate that protecting the entire northern frontage with rock armour would cost in the region of forty million pounds, a sum that neither the council nor central government has indicated any willingness to provide. Were such funding to be found, the defences would need to be maintained and eventually replaced, at further expense, for as long as anyone wished to keep the village where it is. And even then, by deflecting the waves, they would be likely to accelerate erosion further along the coast, at the expense of our neighbours in Brackley.

The alternative, which is known in the jargon as managed realignment, is to plan for a gradual and orderly move inland. This would mean identifying land, safe for at least a century, on which homes, the school and the lifeboat station could be rebuilt over the coming decades, and supporting households through the transition. It would also mean accepting that some of what we love will, in time, be lost.

We do not pretend that this is a painless option. If we had begun planning thirty years ago, when the warning signs first appeared, we would be in a far stronger position today, with land already secured and funds already set aside. We did not, and nor did the authorities responsible for us. That is a reason for urgency, not for despair.

We therefore ask the council for three things. First, that it commit to a long-term plan for Saltmere, developed with residents rather than imposed upon them. Second, that it identify and secure suitable land for relocation within the next five years. Third, that it establish a fund to compensate households whose homes are lost, so that no family is left to bear that burden alone. Should these steps not be taken, we fear that the village will face the worst of both worlds: neither protected nor prepared, simply waiting for the next storm.

To our fellow residents, we say this. Were the choice between staying and leaving entirely ours, many of us would stay. It is not. The sea is making that choice, slowly and without consulting anyone. What remains in our hands is whether we respond to it together, with time to plan, or separately, in emergency, one collapsed garden at a time.
Saltmere has survived for eight hundred years because its people adapted. Its church moved once before. We believe it can do so again, provided we begin now.
Yours sincerely,
The Saltmere Coastal Forum

title: The Language I Wish I Had Kept
focus: Unreal past: wish, if only, it's (high) time, would rather, as if
paragraphs: My grandmother spoke to her hens in Galician. She spoke to the priest, the postman and my mother in Spanish, but the hens, the cow and, when she thought nobody was listening, the photograph of my grandfather on the dresser all received the language she had grown up with in a village in the hills above Lugo. I would hear it through the kitchen door, low and musical, and I understood perhaps one word in five. I wish now that I had understood the rest.

It was not that she refused to teach me. It was rather that nobody thought it worth teaching. My mother, who had moved to Madrid at seventeen, had spent years trying to lose her accent, and she regarded Galician, with the particular impatience of the recently escaped, as a language of poverty and mud. If only she had seen it differently. But I understand why she did not. For her generation, getting on meant getting out, and getting out meant sounding as if you had always been somewhere else.

So I grew up with Spanish, and later English, and a handful of Galician words that I used without knowing they were Galician: the name for a particular kind of drizzle, a word for the feeling of being homesick for a place you have never left, an expression my grandmother used whenever I was being stubborn. I assumed for years that everyone knew them. When I discovered, at university, that my friends from Valencia and Seville had no idea what I was talking about, I felt a strange mixture of embarrassment and pride, as though I had found an unexpected room in a house I thought I knew.

My grandmother died when I was twenty-three. In the weeks afterwards, sorting through her things, I found a bundle of letters she had written to my grandfather during the years he had worked in Switzerland. They were in Galician. I could not read them. I sat on her bed with the letters in my lap and felt, for the first time, the full weight of what had not been passed on. It was as if she had left me a key and I had never learned which door it opened.

I would rather not exaggerate. I have since taken classes, read novels, listened to the radio, and I can now read those letters, slowly, with a dictionary at my elbow. They are not, it turns out, especially dramatic: the price of feed, a neighbour's wedding, a cow that had stopped giving milk. But every so often, in the middle of a list of chores, there is a sentence of such tenderness that I have to put the page down. I would give a great deal to have heard her say those sentences aloud.

Galician, I should add, is not dying. It is spoken by hundreds of thousands of people, taught in schools and broadcast on television, and in many ways it is in better health than it was when my grandmother was young. But languages are not only lost on a national scale. They are lost one family at a time, in kitchens, through a series of small, sensible decisions that nobody intends to be final.

My daughter is seven. She speaks Spanish and English, and she is beginning to learn Galician, mostly from me, mostly badly. Some of my friends find this sweet; others think it is a waste of time she could spend on Mandarin. Perhaps they are right. But it is high time, I think, that somebody in my family stopped making the sensible decision. When she says the word for that particular kind of drizzle, looking out of the window at a grey morning, I hear something I had thought was gone. It is not my grandmother's voice. But it is not entirely unlike it.
